thread.title: After the Bell: Stocks Steamroll Tariff and Job Worries to End Higher

author: Teresa Rivas
title: After the Bell: Stocks Steamroll Tariff and Job Worries to End Higher
text:
By Teresa Rivas Aug. 3, 2018 5:16 p.m. ET Trillion Trumps Tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average built on its midday momentum to end in positive territory Friday. China took steps to discourage shorts from targeting its currency, as it responded with another tariff threat . On the home front, we got a fairly decent jobs report Friday morning, while Apple (AAPL) held onto its trillion-dollar crown . In today's After the Bell , we...
Illustration: Spencer Platt/Getty Images • ...review the jobs data;
• ...examine ongoing earnings strength;
•....check in on Dish Network's (DISH) big gain.
Friday Funday
Stocks ended higher on Friday, brushing off China's latest tariff response and July jobs data .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 136.42 points, or 0.54%, to 25462.58, while the S&P 500 rose 13.13 points, or 0.46%, to 2840.35. The Nasdaq Composite added 9.33 points, or 0.12%, to finish at 7812.01.
The U.S. added slightly fewer jobs than expected in July, but the June figure was revised up. Parsing the data further, Commonwealth Financial Network's Brad McMillian says that while July was a miss, the details show that "we’re still in pretty good shape jobs-wise. It may raise the stakes for coming months, but "the overall trend and underlying data are significantly more positive, and conditions remain healthy overall."
The Conference Board notes that it shows an ongoing diversion between manual labor and office jobs. "The data tells us a story of two labor markets: significant labor shortages for blue-collar workers versus moderate tightness in white-collar jobs." Lazard Asset Management's Ronald Temple notes that the "real puzzle is why wage growth remains sluggish in spite of an ever-tighter labor market," a situation that some argue can't last forever .
In terms of the Federal Reserve, Stifel's Lindsey Piegza argues that Friday's report "continues to support the notion of strong job gains and a continued gradual rate pathway."
Of course, jobs weren't the only issue Friday. China, as expected, made its response to the U.S.'s latest tariff volley. UBS's Erin Browne writes that we should expect ongoing tensions between the U.S. and China to rise in coming months — and market volatility as tariffs increasingly make themselves felt. While rising input costs and export levels may be easy to measure, it could be trickier to quantify the indirect effects of tariffs, including supply chain disruption and depressing effects on business sentiment, "leading to a potential decline in investment and employment."
That said, she sees reason for optimism in global stocks, especially in emerging markets, as the "combination of a stable dollar, China’s stimulus, still solid global growth and earnings should provide a cushion amid non-negligible trade risks."
And we're still in the thick of earnings season, too. We're on track for another quarter of more than 20% earnings per share growth, given the companies that have reported so far. "Strength has been broad-based, with revenues topping forecasts in all 11 sectors, 10 of 11 (save Energy) on earnings," writes Credit Suisse's Jonathan Golub . "Company guidance has been quite positive, leading to upward revisions for both the third quarter and calendar year 2018."
While some bears may claim that most of the growth stems from companies reaping the benefits of tax reform, Guild Investment Management argues that that's not the case: Tax benefits have contributed to just 7.7% of the 23.3% annualized earnings growth S&P 500 companies have notched to date, and "15.5% growth ex-tax benefits is still excellent."
It's hard to argue with that.
The Hot Stock
Dish Network (DISH) shot to the top of the S&P 500 after a solid Pay TV subscriber results in the second quarter.
The shares of shares of the satellite-television were up $4.53, or 14.5%, to $34.20.
The company reported a profit of 83 cents a share, beating forecasts for 81 cents, on sales of $3.46 billion, topping expectations for $3.44 billion. “We raise our 12-month target price by $4 to $30,” said CFRA analyst Tuna N. Amobi .
The shares have lost 28.3% year to date and 43.6% for the past year. — Varada Bhat

The Biggest Loser
Stericycle (SRCL) tumbled to the bottom of the index after it reported lackluster second-quarter results and lowered its full-year forecast.
The medical waste disposal and secure information destruction firm was down $9.31 or 13.1%, to $61.65.
“The more important event for long-term investors was the decision to seek strategic alternatives for the CRS (communications/recall) business, as we anticipated,” said Raymond James analyst Lawrence Keusch . “We believe a sale of CRS would be a positive, allowing management to focus on the core waste collections businesses.” He maintains a Market Perform rating.
The shares have lost 9.3% year to date and 21.4% for the past year. — V.B.
